chapter: Joining Carter and Goodman in New York
title: Personnel of Wilson's big band
summary: Wilson lists his sidemen: Rudy Powell, Pete Clark, Ben Webster, Karl George, Harold Baker, Floyd Beatty and Jake Wiley.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Yes sir. Now talking about that big band of yours, Teddy -- did we mention the personalities yet? We talked about some of them.

Rudy Powell was the lead alto, and third alto doubling on the baritone sax was Pete Clark, who had been with the Chick Webb before that, and on second tenor was George Irish from Boston, who was not a great soloist, but a great section man, and then Ben Webster on first tenor. And then in the brass section, I had Karl George on trumpet.
Yeah, mention something about him, because he was fabulous.

Yeah, he was a fabulous trumpet player, and I don't know what happened to Karl; I think after my band broke up, I think he went with Stan Kenton for awhile, and then I lost track of him. And then my other trumpet player that I was so proud of was Harold Baker, who --

He was discovered by Don Redman in those days, and of course Shorty went on to become very famous playing for Duke, and unfortunately, he died a young man. But he had one of the most beautiful tones of that day on trumpet. And the lead parts that Harold played were

really classics.
And then the trombones, I had from Pittsburgh, Floyd Beatty -- we called him Stumpy, a little fellow, playing trombone.

MR. WILSON: Well, Stumpy goes back to those days with the Zach White band, and he was with one of those bands. And then my other trombone player was -- and I'm very proud of him, Jake Wiley from Detroit. He was playing a technique on the trombone that is still in vogue to this day. He was one of the area players, being taught by a man in Detroit, Bobby Byrne's father -- Bobby Byrne, a white trombone player, was creating quite a bit of comment among musicians in New York in those days, he had organized his band and used the slide for jazz.
Yeah. But Bobby Byrne's father, he had a reputation for being a most generous and most democratic man, even more than his son.
In that he helped so many great musicians, black and white.
Yeah. Well, Jake Wiley was one of the people Bobby's father helped. And we mentioned JC on the drums and Al Casey was on the guitar, and Al Hall on bass.
